title: The Design System an Organisation Can Actually Hold
subtitle: Tokens, enforcement and governance, derived from how the company works rather than from the canon

cv.label: Download CV (PDF)
cv.note: Tailored for the Lead Design Systems role

bio.short: Design leadership in enterprise and consumer software, with the design system in my brief in each of the last three roles. At Bibel TV it ships as an API. Tokens in four tiers, one commit reaching every platform, and a build that refuses work which has left the system.
bio.long:
I lead product design, and in each of my last three roles the design system was part of the brief. Datameer, then Ninox, and now Bibel TV, where the last year has gone almost entirely into it.

The Bibel TV system is not the one a textbook would draw, and that is the most useful thing about it. Product managers and product owners set direction, engineering sits at external agencies, and the people building with the system are not designers. When I arrived, nothing in the app was tokenized. Every change went through an agency, priced in hours and scheduled into a sprint. A card radius. A font size. Small changes were not small.

So the token architecture is a control surface rather than a taxonomy. Four tiers: primitives, semantic, component, and page or view. The top two add no new values at all. They alias downward, and that redundancy is the point. Each is a place the company can change spacing, type size or radius itself, without an agency release. It is also the first step toward server-driven UI for the streaming part of the app.

The part I find most telling is that the agency backed it. The architecture takes billable change work away from them, and they were enthusiastic anyway. That is the only kind of authority available to me there, and it is the kind I have most practice at.

Above the tokens sits the enforcement. Checks run identically on a laptop and in CI, and they refuse work that has left the system. Two of them catch a token reference that does not resolve and a color written straight into a component. Neither shows up as a visual difference, so the build is the only place they surface. Storybook is the shared surface, because the people prototyping with it are product managers and engineers.

Accessibility sits inside the same instinct, and the ChurchDesk work is the part I would point at. We audited our own website and also the websites customers build with the platform, for EU Accessibility Act compliance. The second half is the harder one. Those sites are made by parish staff, not by specialists, so the standard has to hold in output nobody trained for. I shipped AI alt-text generation there too, across six countries. Screen-reader semantics and ARIA are standing practice for me, at Bibel TV as well as ChurchDesk and Ninox.

The color engine is the same idea one layer down. K-means clustering in OKLCH rather than RGB, so themes carry even perceptual weight. WCAG contrast is validated inside the algorithm, so no theme can ship failing it.

I would not propose this same architecture at Telekom. It answers one company's constraints. A 230,000-person telco's are different: many product teams, many vendors, a large legacy surface, and a brand that has to hold across all of it. What transfers is the habit of deriving the system from the organization rather than from the canon, and of saying what each decision costs.

context.emphasis: Lead with judgement, not with the tier count. The Bibel TV architecture answers how that company actually works rather than how the canon says to build one. Engineering sits at external agencies, product managers and product owners set direction, and the people who build with the system are product managers and engineers. He says so plainly, including that it would not be right for Telekom. For a 230,000-person telco with many teams and many vendors, reading an organization and building what it can hold is the transferable skill. The tiers are evidence for it. Then T4, T7, T9 and T11: tokens, enforcement, tooling. Then influence without a reporting line, which T5 and T15 ask for as the job itself. Accessibility as a practice, with the ChurchDesk audit as the lead. Mentoring shown as a decade of it, which directly answers T15.
